target_customer: Smartphone owners who wanted to swap contacts and later photos by physically bumping phones
problem: Exchanging contact details or photos between phones was slow and manual; Bump used the accelerometer and a server match so two phones bumped together swapped data.
business_model: Free consumer app; monetization was never achieved
product_category: Mobile contact and file sharing app, later photo sharing

founders.name: David Lieb
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder/CEO and now a YC Group Partner who led Google Photos after the acquisition. No education or prior employers on the page.

exit.reason: Bump and Flock apps were shut down on 2014-01-31 after the acquisition; the team moved to other projects.

technical_complexity.rationale: Reliable detection of a physical bump by phone sensors matched through a server with location and timing, scaled to millions of users on a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Value rose with installed base, but the core gesture was replicable by platform owners, and Apple added AirDrop in iOS 7.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Apple's AirDrop in iOS 7 eroded the file sharing use case. Google bought Bump in September 2013 and shut the apps in January 2014.

market_need_then: Smartphone adoption was rising in 2009 and the iPhone App Store had just opened, but contact swapping was a convenience rather than a painful job. Demand showed as large install counts: the YC description states more than 150M installs by 2013.

branding.domain_note: Company site was bumptechnologies.com; the bump.com domain history was not found.

identity.voice_and_tone: Playful fist bump gesture used in press coverage.

branding.brand_signature: The physical fist bump gesture between two phones.
branding.community_and_virality: Press coverage drew on the fist bump gesture, and the app was called out as a top mobile app and a noted download milestone; Bump opened an API to developers in February 2010.

brand_strength.rationale: A memorable verb name matching the gesture, with large installs and wide press coverage, though it did not build a lasting business.

pivots.to: Bump and Flock photo and file sharing
pivots.why: Extended the app to photos, videos and files; Flock was an automatic shared album app.

outcome_analysis: Bump grew to more than 150 million installs on the viral gesture and raised about $19.5 million from Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz, but never monetized. Apple's AirDrop in iOS 7 undercut the core use. Google acquired the company in September 2013 at a reported $30 million or more and shut Bump and Flock on 2014-01-31, while the unreleased Photoroll app became the basis of Google Photos, so the real value was the team and that product. Other success factor: the team's later product became Google Photos.
notes: Competitors dated near March 2009 were not found, so the list is left empty; commenters likened it to Palm infrared beaming. Series A is reported as $3M to $3.5M and dated October or November 2009 by different outlets. Series B is $16M per TechCrunch, another listing says $16.5M. Purchase price was never official, reports range from $30M to $60M so amount is null. Total raised estimates vary between about $19.9M and $50.6M. Jake Mintz is named as a cofounder by one search snippet but not on the YC page, so not listed. Founder education and prior employers were not found. The company site returned a 503. The Bump name origin was not found.
